name: Low-glycemic diet for acne

lead: A low-glycemic diet swaps fast-digesting carbohydrates such as white bread, sugary drinks and sweets for slower ones such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables. People with acne use it hoping for fewer breakouts and clearer skin without drugs.

The proposed chain is that high-glycemic meals raise blood glucose and insulin, which is thought to raise IGF-1 and androgen activity, and in turn sebum production and comedone formation. Wikipedia's acne article reports several randomized and non-randomized studies in which lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne severity, and dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars. The body of evidence is described as emerging.

paras: People rebuild meals around legumes, whole grains, vegetables and fewer sweets and refined starches, and keep it up as an everyday eating pattern. Skin changes are typically assessed over weeks to a few months.

A low-glycemic eating pattern is an ordinary dietary approach with no specific safety concerns identified in the sources. Glycemic index is an imperfect measure: some low-GI foods are high in fat or sugar, and values vary between individuals and preparations.

angle.text: A low-glycemic diet keeps blood sugar rising slowly, which is thought to lower insulin and oil-gland signalling and lead to fewer breakouts and clearer skin. Several randomized and non-randomized studies have reported lower acne severity on lower-glycemic-load diets.

lead: A low-glycemic diet (low-GI or low-glycemic-load diet) is an eating pattern built around carbohydrates that raise blood glucose slowly, such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables, in place of white bread, sugary drinks and sweets. People use it to get clearer skin: the idea is that steadier glucose and insulin levels lead to fewer breakouts and less oily skin, without drugs.[1][2]

The glycemic index, introduced by David Jenkins and colleagues in 1981, ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 against pure glucose, and glycemic load adjusts that ranking for portion size.[3] Wikipedia's acne article reports that randomized and non-randomized studies have found lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne, and that dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars; it also describes the diet-and-acne evidence as emerging.[1]

Several small randomized trials have measured lesion counts, hormones and skin biopsies on low-glycemic-load diets in people with acne, with reductions in lesion counts reported in 10 to 12 week studies.[2][4][5] Glycemic index itself has recognized limitations: values depend on ripeness, cooking and processing, and individual responses differ.[3]

paras: The glycemic index rates carbohydrate-containing foods by their effect on blood glucose over two hours relative to a reference such as glucose; foods scoring 55 or less are classed as low, 56 to 69 as medium and 70 or more as high.[3] Glycemic load multiplies GI by the grams of carbohydrate in a serving and divides by 100.[3]

A low-glycemic diet for acne emphasizes low-GI carbohydrates and reduces refined, high-GI items. No single standard version exists; trial diets have ranged from low-GI carbohydrate with higher protein to plain low-GL advice.[2][4]

Proponents and some clinicians propose that high-glycemic meals produce larger insulin responses, which are thought to raise IGF-1 and androgen activity, increasing sebum production and follicular blockage.[1] Wikipedia notes that androgens and IGF-1 both appear to be essential for acne, since acne does not develop in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome or in Laron syndrome, which involves low IGF-1.[1]

A 2007 randomized trial in 43 males aged 15 to 25 compared a diet of about 25% protein and 45% low-GI carbohydrate with a carbohydrate-dense control diet for 12 weeks. Lesion counts fell more in the low-glycemic-load group, which also lost more weight and improved insulin sensitivity; the authors noted that weight loss may have contributed.[2] A second 2007 randomized, investigator-masked trial of 43 male patients with a high-protein, low-glycemic-load diet reported greater lesion reduction, a lower free androgen index and higher IGFBP-1, again with weight loss as a possible contributor.[4]

A 2012 Korean randomized trial in 32 patients with mild to moderate acne ran 10 weeks. The low-glycemic-load group had fewer inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions, and biopsies showed smaller sebaceous glands, less inflammation and lower SREBP-1 and IL-8 expression.[5] A 2018 randomized trial in 66 adults with moderate to severe acne found that IGF-1 fell significantly after two weeks on a low GI/GL diet, while glucose, insulin and body composition did not differ; the authors called for longer studies.[6]

Many larger low-GI trials have studied diabetes and weight rather than skin, for example a meta-analysis of low-GI diets in diabetes management.[7] The acne trials are small and short, and the field is described as emerging.[1]

Wikipedia lists several caveats: GI values change with ripeness and cooking, individual responses vary from day to day, GI ignores portion size and insulin response, and some low-GI foods such as chocolate cake and ice cream are not otherwise considered healthy.[3] A 2023 Cochrane review, cited there, found low-GI or low-GL diets did not produce more weight loss in overweight adults than other approaches.[3]

timeline.event: David Jenkins and colleagues introduce the glycemic index.[3]
Two randomized trials of low-glycemic-load diets in young men with acne are published.[2][4]
Korean randomized trial reports lower lesion counts and smaller sebaceous glands on a low-glycemic-load diet.[5]
Two-week randomized trial reports lower IGF-1 in adults with moderate to severe acne.[6]
